evidence.limitations: Quidra is a small, early-stage first-party language ecosystem (github.com/quidra-lang). Evidence is drawn from the project's own specification/architecture docs (embedded in this task packet) plus its public GitHub README and a companion WASM playground repository, cross-checked with a bounded set of web searches for an official editor-marketplace extension. Absence of a marketplace listing in search results is treated as evidence of absence rather than a search-recall gap, consistent with the same search depth budget used for other languages in this evaluation.

component_scores.dedicated_profiler_tooling: 0/20 (no profiler command or integration documented anywhere)
component_scores.sanitizer_or_diagnostic_instrumentation: 8/20 (ASan/UBSan instrumentation exists for generated programs, but documentation frames it around compiler CI rather than a general user-facing debugging/profiling workflow)

raw_findings: GitHub README states: 'quidra build --debug asks the native Clang driver for an unoptimized, frame-pointer-preserving debug build and disables link-time dead stripping for that build.'
Same source: 'quidra debug FILE.qui launches LLDB or GDB (or QUIDRA_DEBUGGER) against that executable,' confirming real integration with mainstream native debuggers rather than a bespoke one.

The same README passage explicitly disclaims full source mapping: 'Current integration guarantees native function/symbol visibility; fine-grained Quidra source-line DWARF mapping is not yet claimed,' meaning breakpoints/stepping are only guaranteed at the native symbol level, not reliable Quidra-source-line granularity.
No dedicated profiler command, sampling/tracing profiler, or memory-profiler integration is documented anywhere in the spec, architecture doc, or README.

The architecture spec notes that 'Sanitizer development builds propagate AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer instrumentation to generated native programs as well as the compiler,' but frames this primarily as a compiler CI mechanism for exercising retain/release, pin/unpin, bounds, and drop paths rather than a documented, user-facing profiling workflow.
metric.debugger_profiler_support.rubric: Frozen 5-component proxy, 20 pts each, applied identically across all 10 languages: (1) a native debug-build compiler flag exists; (2) a standard-debugger integration command exists (wraps a mainstream debugger); (3) source-level (language-line) debug-info mapping (DWARF or equivalent) is claimed/verified; (4) a dedicated profiler tool or integration exists (sampling/tracing/memory profiler); (5) sanitizer or comparable runtime-instrumentation support is available for user-facing diagnosis.
metric.debugger_profiler_support.total: ~48/100 using the frozen rubric, recorded here as 45 after rounding for consistency with the qualitative weight given to the explicit source-line-mapping disclaimer and complete absence of profiler tooling

component_scores.additional_first_party_tooling: 18/20 (working WASM playground plus structured inspect/patch API, genuinely usable by tooling/LLM clients even though it does not execute programs)
component_scores.lsp_feature_depth: 7/20 (2 of 6 tracked features -- diagnostics and formatting -- documented; completion/hover/go-to-def/rename not documented)
component_scores.official_lsp_exists: 12/20 (present but explicitly framed as an initial/partial implementation)
component_scores.syntax_highlighting_artifact: 5/20 (only inside the bespoke playground web editor; no portable grammar package found)

raw_findings: The repo documents a real 'quidra lsp' command described as 'a thin client of the ordinary compiler frontend, not a second parser or type system' with explicitly 'Initial LSP support' limited to protocol-default UTF-16 positions, full-document synchronization, push diagnostics, and document formatting.

GitHub README text confirms the same surface: quidra check --json, quidra fmt (+ --check), quidra lsp ('provides compiler-backed diagnostics and formatting over standard LSP stdio framing'), quidra inspect (with --no-source/--no-effects/--kind/--depth filters), and quidra patch.
No completion, hover, go-to-definition, or rename capability is documented anywhere in the spec or README for the LSP server.

A first-party browser Playground (quidra-lang/playground) exists, running the real compiler frontend compiled to WebAssembly, offering in-editor diagnostics with codes/ranges, formatting, typed-IR view, structural inspect (node ids/kinds/spans/hashes/types), and hash-checked patch application -- but it explicitly excludes program execution ('No Run, REPL, JIT or any other execution'), multi-file editing, and package management.

A search for an official Quidra VS Code/JetBrains/Open VSX marketplace extension returned no matching listing; only unrelated languages (e.g. Quil, Quint, Q#, q) were found under similar-sounding names.
No dedicated TextMate/semantic-highlighting grammar package for Quidra was found distributed independently of the playground's own embedded editor.
metric.ide_editor_support_quality.rubric: Frozen 5-component proxy, 20 pts each, applied identically across all 10 languages: (1) an official/compiler-backed LSP exists; (2) LSP feature depth (diagnostics, formatting, completion, hover, go-to-definition, rename -- prorated by count of documented features out of 6); (3) an official editor extension is published on a mainstream marketplace (VS Code Marketplace / Open VSX / JetBrains Marketplace); (4) syntax/semantic highlighting is available through a first-party or official artifact; (5) additional first-party interactive/editor-adjacent tooling (browser playground, structured inspect/patch APIs consumable by tooling).
